case_analysis.focal_point: Whether ADA Title II and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act claims in the elementary and secondary education context require plaintiffs to prove 'bad faith or gross misjudgment' by school officials, or whether the standard discrimination framework applicable in all other contexts should apply.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (42 U.S.C. § 12131 et seq.), Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (29 U.S.C. § 794), and the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), as they intersect in the context of educational services for students with disabilities.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner A.J.T., a student with disabilities, argues that the heightened 'bad faith or gross misjudgment' standard applied by the Eighth Circuit is an judicially invented requirement that has no basis in the text of Title II or Section 504, improperly adds an extra element to discrimination claims exclusively in the school context, and conflicts with the Supreme Court's statutory interpretation principles requiring consistent application of the same statutory language across all contexts. Petitioner, supported by the United States as amicus curiae, contends that the standard ADA and Rehabilitation Act discrimination framework should apply uniformly, regardless of whether the claim arises in an educational setting governed by IDEA.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent Osseo Area Schools argues that because IDEA already provides a comprehensive statutory scheme guaranteeing appropriate educational services to students with disabilities, applying the standard ADA/Section 504 discrimination framework in the IDEA context would create an unworkable overlap between the two statutory schemes. Respondents contend that the 'bad faith or gross misjudgment' standard appropriately reflects the 'conceptual peculiarity' that arises when ADA and Section 504 claims are brought in the specific context of IDEA-governed educational services, effectively preventing plaintiffs from using the ADA and Rehabilitation Act to relitigate IDEA adequacy determinations under a lower threshold.

Martinez forecloses giving identical statutory language different operative meanings across contexts — the 'bad faith or gross misjudgment' standard is a judicial invention with no textual anchor in Title II or Section 504. As Chief Justice, I am mindful that a narrow holding serves institutional legitimacy best: we need not resolve every question about how the standard discrimination framework applies in educational settings, but only that the Eighth Circuit's heightened standard is impermissible. The strongest counterargument — that IDEA's comprehensive scheme implicitly warrants a different standard — is adequately answered by Congress's own savings clause in 20 U.S.C. § 1415(l), which expressly preserves ADA and Section 504 rights, and by the availability of IDEA's exhaustion requirement to manage duplicative litigation concerns without rewriting the substantive elements of a separate statute.

Justice Alito's point about 20 U.S.C. § 1415(l) is particularly compelling from a textual standpoint: Congress expressly provided that IDEA shall not be construed to restrict rights under the ADA and Section 504, which means the Eighth Circuit's heightened standard not only lacks textual grounding in Title II and Section 504 but affirmatively contradicts an explicit congressional directive in IDEA itself. The strongest argument for the respondent — that IDEA's comprehensive educational framework implicitly warrants a higher threshold to prevent relitigation of adequacy determinations — fails because Congress addressed the relationship between these statutes directly through IDEA's exhaustion provisions, and it is not the judiciary's role to supplement that congressional judgment with a judicially invented substantive standard. As I have long maintained, when the statutory text is clear, our inquiry begins and ends there, and neither the text of Title II nor Section 504 contains any language supporting a context-specific heightened intent requirement.

But as Justice Kagan correctly notes, Congress addressed this concern directly through IDEA's exhaustion requirements and savings clauses — it is not the judiciary's role to further restructure the statutory scheme by inventing a heightened burden that the text does not support.
